name: Silacayoapan Mixtec
sweep_summary: Silacayoapan Mixtec (sila1250) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Carroll 2015 (UCSD PhD, Ixpantepec Nieves variety, Glottolog-linked to sila1250), was already on file (fetched sources by the mixt1425 sweep from eScholarship/CORE) and was read: it is a first-hand phonological and acoustic study giving fixed default stress on the first syllable of the bimoraic root couplet (trochaic foot aligned to the root; prefixes/clitics never stressed; correlates duration, intensity, periodicity), pp. 98-99. Through its bibliography the primary description of Silacayoapan proper, North & Shields 1977 (SIL PIL 54, pp. 21-33; data from San Jerónimo Progreso), was located in the Merrifield 1977 volume already on file from the sanm1301 sweep; pp. 21 and 31-33 were scanned. It states 'Word stress is on the first syllable of the couplet' (p. 21) with a stress-plus-H-tone shift onto the couplet's second syllable before single-vowel person enclitics on non-verb couplets (p. 31, Rule 4), which Carroll re-analyses as a perceptual effect. Both first-hand sources agree on root-couplet-initial stress; nothing remains unread. only web lookups/curl were used (Glottolog record 569742 confirmed the sila1250 link; eScholarship returned empty to automated fetch, SIL and DuckDuckGo fetches were blocked).

new_statements.quote: The phonological word, with the couplet as its basis, may have several syllables either preceding or following the couplet. Word stress is on the first syllable of the couplet. [...] (p. 31) When these vowel clusters are formed by the postposing of single-vowel enclitic person markers, the stress of the couplet is shifted to the syllable immediately preceding that of the enclitic, and the tone of the syllable receiving the stress becomes high.
new_statements.citation: North, Joanne & Jana Shields. 1977. Silacayoapan Mixtec phonology. In William R. Merrifield (ed.), Studies in Otomanguean phonology (SIL Publications in Linguistics 54), 21-33. Dallas: SIL / UT Arlington.
new_statements.locator: p. 21 (PDF page 29), introductory section before sec. 1 Consonants; exception on p. 31 (PDF page 39), sec. 4 Morphophonemics, Rule 4
new_statements.reading: Fixed word stress on the first syllable of the bimoraic root couplet (initial stress of the root, not of the phonological word: pre-couplet prefixes/proclitics and post-couplet enclitics are unstressed). One morphologically conditioned exception: a single-vowel person enclitic (/i/ 1s, /e/) on a non-verb couplet moves stress one syllable rightward onto the couplet's second syllable, which also takes H tone. Carroll 2015 (pp. 98-99), the fuller first-hand study of the Ixpantepec Nieves variety under the same glottocode, confirms couplet-initial (root-initial) trochaic stress with acoustic evidence and argues the enclitic 'shift' is a perceptual effect of tone contour and vowel fusion rather than a stress shift. Both sources agree on the default: stress on the first syllable of the root couplet.

sources.quote: p. 21: "The phonological word, with the couplet as its basis, may have several syllables either preceding or following the couplet. Word stress is on the first syllable of the couplet. In examples, the couplet precedes space or hyphen (-)." p. 31: "One further morphophonemic process takes place when /i/ or /e/ are postposed to a nonverbal couplet. When these vowel clusters are formed by the postposing of single-vowel enclitic person markers, the stress of the couplet is shifted to the syllable immediately preceding that of the enclitic, and the tone of the syllable receiving the stress becomes high."

sources.note: First-hand description of Silacayoapan Mixtec proper (San Jerónimo Progreso): word stress on the first syllable of the (bimoraic) couplet, the couplet being the nucleus of the phonological word with unstressed syllables possible before and after it. Morphophonemic exception: a single-vowel enclitic person marker (/i/, /e/) on a nonverbal couplet shifts stress to the couplet's second syllable (now immediately before the enclitic) and that syllable takes high tone (examples hata 'back' > hatá-i 'my back', ve'e 'house' > ve'é-i 'my house'). Carroll 2015 re-analyses the same phenomenon in Nieves…

sources.quote: Nieves Mixtec maintains a close parallelism between the morphological structure and the prosodic structure. In the minimal word, consisting only of a bimoraic root, stress falls on the first syllable as in (4.20). [...] The position of stress is fixed, as it does not change with the addition of monomoraic functional morphemes. [...] In contrast to the stress system described for Silacayoapan Mixtec (North & Shields 1977), mentioned in §4.2, in Nieves Mixtec the stress is maintained on the first syllable of the root even when the 1s enclitic /=ì/ is added to the root, as in (4.25).
sources.locator: Sec. 4.3.2 'Stress placement', pp. 98-99; also abstract p. xx-xxi, sec. 4.2.1 p. 86-87, pp. 100-101 (trimoraic words), ch. 5 acoustics, conclusion pp. 271-272
sources.note: First-hand phonological and acoustic description of the Ixpantepec Nieves variety (Glottolog places it under sila1250). Default stress on the first syllable of the bimoraic root/couplet (a CVV root forms one heavy stressed syllable); trochaic foot aligned to the root; prefixes and clitics are unstressable and never shift stress; lexicalised trimoraic prefix+root words stress the etymological root (= penultimate mora). The apparent stress shift onto the 1s enclitic reported for Silacayoapan proper is analysed as a perceptual effect of a HL contour plus vowel fusion (p. 91, p. 100 n.5). Acousti…
